title: Positional-decay and MoE sparsity benchmarking (on-prem performance review)
summary: Deep technical review of positional embedding scaling (ROPE/rotary decay), MoE sparsity economics for hybrid on-prem deployment, and practical KV cache sharding strategies to hit p99 latency targets. Reviewed quantization tradeoffs and proposed a small-scale benchmark plan to validate tail latency under realistic token affinity. Next steps include sharing benchmark sheet, running an on-prem pilot with 2-node shard, and a security checklist for KMS integration.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-10 14:30 UTC
Duration: 78 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Diego Ramos (Redwood Infra), Martin Lopez (DataForge Infra), Sofia Chen (DataForge ML), Ravi Patel (DataForge Security), Amara Okafor (DataForge Platform)

0:00 Alex: hey everyone thanks for carving out the time, um the plan today is a fairly tactical deep dive on positional embeddings and MoE cost tradeoffs for your on-prem run, we'll try and keep it practical and leave time for the benchmark plan at the end
0:24 Martin: sounds good, we mostly want to validate p99 tail at 2k context and also understand cost on routing when we enable Sparsity-at-Scale
0:42 Priya: quick clarifying q — by sparsity do you mean MoE top-k gating (k=2 or k=4) or mixture configurations? because cost delta is big between the two
1:05 Martin: mainly top-2 today but we want to try top-4 in a follow up; and we're curious if positional decay (rope) adjustment helps with longer context so we don't blow up K-V cache size
1:22 Sofia: short background — we have a Llama-derived model and a Mistral-style 7B variant, and a Qwen-ish 14B in eval. We're exploring MoE layers stiched into the middle of the stack for bursty workloads. We run everything inside our VPC and plan to keep KV cache on local NVMe attached to the nodes
2:02 Diego: quick infra note — NVMe has fast IO but we want to avoid cross-host KV lookups. so sharding/affinity matters a lot, otherwise permutation kills latency
2:19 Alex: ok, let's start with ROPE. the core idea — rotary embeddings decay and effective sequence identity as length grows, you can scale the ROPE frequency/decay factor to preserve locality for longer contexts but it changes the model's positional interpolation. we saw in our experiments that a mild decay factor — about 0.85 on the high-frequency bands — keeps KV reuse high without retraining for many models
3:10 Priya: adding, in practice you often trade a bit of generation coherence for much better KV hit rate. there was a Mistral-ish case where the p50 stayed same but p99 improved 25% after small rope freq retune
3:38 Martin: is that just a config tweak, or do we need to recompile kernels or re-quantize?
3:45 Priya: mostly a model-side rotary scaling change; you can patch weights with a small adapter that rescales the rotary coefficients at runtime — no kernel changes needed. quantization can amplify artifacts though, so worth testing quant profiles
4:12 Sofia: re: quant — we've tried 4-bit GPTQ on the 14B Qwen-like and saw weird hallucination spikes and longer tail latency when we enabled group-scoped quantization. anyone seen that?
4:28 Alex: yeah quant can introduce more variability in step-time. two notes: (1) use per-channel or per-block qconfig if available; (2) increase KV cache prefetch window for quantized runs so you avoid on-the-fly dequant+repack stalls
5:02 Priya: also we recommend dynamic fallback for safety — keep a smaller float32 path you can fall back to for requests flagged as high-risk (security prompts, high cost SLAs)
5:26 Ravi: on the security front we need KMS and HSM guidance. we can't ship customer IVF or anything that leaks secrets; how do you handle KMS on private control planes?
5:42 Alex: short answer — we integrate with customer KMS via key-wrap; for on-prem we can support bring-your-own-hsm via PKCS#11 and we store only wrapped keys in the control plane. I'll attach our security pack. (link provided in chat)
6:08 Martin: great, back to MoE routing — if we enable top-2, what's the effective token routing cost? are we paying full expert forward for every token?
6:25 Priya: depends on implementation. Redwood's hybrid routing allows a cheap router stage — we can do a prefilter where ~60% of tokens are routed to just one expert (w/score threshold) and 40% to two. real cost model should use token-affinity histogram not just average tokens/sec
7:00 Priya: i'll sketch the math: cost = base_model_cost + routing_overhead + expert_forward_cost * fraction_routed. if experts are sparse and smaller, net cost can be lower than dense models at high throughput due to fewer FLOPs per token
7:28 Sofia: question — for on-prem, is it possible to colocate the router and experts to avoid cross-host hops for hot tokens? we've seen network jitter kill p99
7:42 Diego: yes colocating hot shards helps, we use a placement strategy called affinity-shard where token hash + user-id mapping tries to keep the same session routed to same host. downside is imbalance during spikes
8:05 Alex: that's where autoscaling + eviction policies come in. we can autoscale expert pools for bursts and fall back to a compatible dense variant when cold experts are missing. the runtime supports transparent fallback with rollout policies
8:28 Martin: curious about ROPE + MoE interaction — does extending ROPE to longer contexts change routing behavior? ie token positions matter for gating?
8:44 Priya: in some gating networks positional features are part of the router input so yes, if ROPE changes relative position embeddings routers can shift which tokens trigger experts. we had a case where pushing rope frequency increased routing diversity which actually increased total expert forwards by 12%
9:13 Sofia: so it's a double-edged sword — better long-range context but potentially higher routing cost
9:22 Alex: exactly. that's why benchmarking should capture token-affinity traces and positional distribution. simple uniform token tests will miss it
9:40 Martin: let's talk KV cache sharding — you mentioned affinity-shard earlier, can you walk through a recommended sharding plan for 2-4 node on-prem cluster?
9:55 Priya: sure. for two nodes we recommend a primary-secondary affinity pattern: each session hashes to a primary node; if primary is under load you can mirror a hot window to secondary. for four nodes you want consistent hashing with a small replication factor (1.2x) to balance while keeping most hits local. avoid full replication, it's terrible for write throughput
10:28 Diego: implementation detail — NVMe is local and fast, but the lookup code needs to be async and GPU-aware; otherwise the CPU-GPU sync kills token throughput
10:42 Martin: does Redwood runtime do KV prefetching based on soft prediction?
10:49 Priya: yes we have a predictive prefetcher that uses recent token affinity and session's recent cache hit patterns. it learns a bit online and is configurable per-model
11:05 Sofia: that sounds promising. do we need to pin sessions to a host if we use predictive prefetch?
11:12 Priya: pinning improves hit rate but reduces elasticity. predictive prefetch with a small replication factor hits a sweet spot for many customers
11:28 Martin: benchmarking — what's the recommended load mix? we have chat-like traffic (short prompts) and long-context summarization.
11:40 Alex: suggested mix: 60% short (avg 64 tokens), 25% medium (512 tokens), 15% long (2k tokens). include a ~5% burst window where 80% of requests touch the same session to simulate hot affinity
12:05 Sofia: about quant again — if we use 4-bit we should expect some p99 widening; is there a recommended safety margin for SLA?
12:18 Priya: from our traces, expect 10-40% p99 inflation depending on qconfig and model family. for mission-critical SLAs we recommend hybrid: quant for steady-state low-cost paths, float fallback for high-p99 requests
12:35 Martin: can we simulate the worst-case where many users access old sessions so KV cache misses spike? how do you measure tail resilience?
12:48 Alex: you run a spike test with session churn: create N sessions stable for T, then churn M% of sessions per minute to emulate cold starts. measure p50/p95/p99 and also token cost per request. we'll include a test harness in the sheet
13:10 Priya: another subtlety — rope decay can reduce effective KV reuse so when you retune, pair that test with real user traces. synthetic long context is not sufficient
13:28 Amara: on provisioning — Diego will need to set up the environment; we want an HSM stub and VPC peering to our control plane for telemetry, while keeping data path fully local
13:40 Diego: we can stub KMS using local HSM emulator for the pilot and enable the real HSM later; network peering for metrics only, no token payloads leave the VPC
13:55 Ravi: that's acceptable. send the security checklist. any compliance implications of storing wrapped keys on the control plane? we need to confirm retention policies
14:05 Alex: we'll attach our compliance doc. we only ever store wrapped key material and we log key unwrap ops in audit logs; you can require HSM-backed unwrapping for sensitive workflows
14:26 Martin: ok next — a concrete benchmark plan and metric targets please
14:33 Alex: propose baseline targets for the pilot: p50 < 40 ms for short prompts, p99 < 250 ms for short prompts; medium p50 < 120 ms, p99 < 450 ms; long context p50 < 350 ms, p99 < 1.2s. cost target is to be lower than cloud-hosted equivalent by 30% for sustained throughput
15:05 Priya: we'll measure routing cost as relative FLOP per token and also show per-token dollar equivalent for your cost model (including host amortization)
15:20 Sofia: how much instrumentation is needed in the model to capture position-dependent routing?
15:27 Priya: add router trace logs that record hash, gating score, selected experts, and positional features. keep sampling to 1% for production, 10% for pilot to limit overhead
15:42 Martin: logging overhead — will that affect tail latency?
15:48 Diego: logging can if synchronous. use async ring-buffers and offload to a sidecar; Redwood runtime supports lightweight in-memory sampling
16:05 Alex: ok wrapping towards an execution plan — we'll run a two-node pilot with these steps: 1) baseline dense runs for each model; 2) enable ROPE tuning adapter for long context; 3) enable MoE top-2 routing with affinity sharding; 4) run quantized 4-bit profile and hybrid fallback; 5) capture metrics and routing histograms
16:28 Sofia: small ask — can we get a prebuilt container image to ensure deterministic kernels? reproducibility matters for us
16:35 Priya: yes we'll provide a container image with pinned kernels and kernel flags used in our internal tests. image link included in the benchmark sheet
16:45 Martin: any gotchas for sealing the NVMe when using KMS? like encrypted FS impacts throughput?
16:53 Diego: encrypted FS will increase CPU overhead; we recommend hardware-backed encryption or using an L4 kernel bypass for NVMe crypto when possible
17:05 Ravi: also confirm audit log retention and where logs are stored; we need evidence for our SOC process
17:12 Alex: will include log retention options in the compliance checklist; you can choose local-only or push to your SIEM over a secure channel
17:25 Amara: timeline — if we start provisioning this week we could run a two-week pilot and meet to review results mid-July
17:33 Alex: sounds good. we'll aim to have configs and sheet by Monday the 14th
17:40 Martin: one last technical question — rope interpolation: any guidance for stepwise vs continuous scaling? we worry about sudden behavior change between context sizes
17:50 Priya: prefer continuous scaling with a smooth decay curve; stepwise jumps can create boundary artifacts. small smooth scaling also makes routing changes gradual which is easier to debug
18:12 Sofia: and if routing diversity increases we can tune gating threshold to bump down expert forwards by 10-15% without hurting quality in many cases
18:25 Alex: ok i think we have enough. quick recap of next steps and action items (see calendar notes). thanks everyone
18:36 Martin: thanks, this was super helpful
18:40 End of recording.
